Hart Circle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three circles carve out eight curved triangles, and another circle can touch four of the little circles drawn inside them.
How to play: Drag a circle, its centre dot or its edge dot; pick a triangle from the drop-down and tick the boxes to see the other circles. Press Reset to start again.

given circles base incircle associated incircles Hart circle

Look for the math

Move the grey circles and watch the coloured ones chase them. Every circle you see is forced by the three grey ones: the green one sits in the curved triangle you chose, the red ones sit in its neighbours, and the blue one just fits between all four.

Eight curved triangles

Three mutually crossing circles can cut the plane into eight regions, one of them reaching off to infinity. Write the two crossing points of circles ci and cj as Ak and A′k, where i + j + k = 6. Because the indices are the distinct numbers 1, 2 and 3, that condition has just one answer: circles c1 and c3 meet at A2 and A′2. The eight sign choices in the drop-down name the eight regions; the logic test samples the board and confirms that all eight really occur.

Straight sides become curved

Start with a triangle whose three sides are lines. Under inversion, a line through the centre becomes another line and every other line becomes a circle through the centre. Inversion keeps angles the same, so a line touching a circle still touches its image. That is how Feuerbach's theorem turns into a statement about curved triangles: the incircle and the excircles of a straight triangle become circles touching the three new ones, and the nine-point circle becomes the Hart circle.

One circle for four neighbours

Pick a base triangle such as A1A2A3. The triangles A′1A2A3, A1A′2A3 and A1A2A′3 each share an arc and two corners with it. The page claims that for every choice of base there is a circle touching the four incircles; this is Hart's theorem, and the Hart circle plays the part of the nine-point circle here. The applet finds each of those circles by solving the problem of Apollonius: there are two tangent solutions, and it keeps the one that also touches the green incircle. The logic test checks all 8 base choices: at the starting position every tangency is exact to six decimal places.

What the old applet really tests

Its tangency test accepts a point within 2 pixels of a circle, so a nearly straight-line arrangement can pass with a small gap: the logic test builds a pair that passes that test while missing exact tangency by one pixel, and checks the generated eight-region arrangements at full precision. The theorem is exact; the drawing's tolerance is not. The applet also computes a "signature" for the two solutions and never uses it — a harmless leftover. Hart Circle is not Hart's inversor: that is a four-bar linkage which turns circular motion into straight-line motion, while this is a circle theorem about curved triangles.

Tick “Show additional circles”, then drag one grey circle right up to another: the blue circle stretches, but it keeps touching the four coloured ones.
